short_version.text: Three ordinary things can sit behind a no-show: the client forgets, nothing is at stake, or cancelling feels harder than not turning up. This playbook fixes each one. Chapter 1 shows what a missed slot costs and the order to act in. Chapter 2 sets a deposit clients accept. Chapter 3 times reminders so they work. Chapter 4 writes a cancellation policy clients respect. Chapter 5 refills the slots that open up from a waitlist. Every figure comes from a dated source listed at the back. Start with reminders this week.

chapters.heading: Cut your no-shows by more than half

sections.text: Send every client an automatic reminder, and ask for a deposit on the bookings that hurt most when they are missed. In appointment data from Example Booking Software customers for July to September 2026, 10.5% of appointments booked with no reminder and no deposit ended in a no-show, against 4.6% of those that got a text and an email reminder [S1, S2]. That is 56% fewer empty slots. Appointments secured with a deposit were missed 2.2% of the time [S3].

The rest of this chapter covers why clients miss, what a missed slot really costs you, and the three fixes in the order to put them in place. The chapters after it go deep on each fix, with the exact wording and settings.
Why do clients not show up for appointments?

Three ordinary things can sit behind a no-show. The booking was made weeks ago, and the day arrives without anything to bring it back to mind. Nothing is at stake, so a busy morning or a bit of rain can tip the balance. And cancelling can feel harder than not turning up: the client would have to call during your opening hours, explain themselves and maybe face a fee, so they say nothing at all.

Each of those has its own fix. A reminder deals with forgetting, and appointments that got one were missed far less often (4.6% against 10.5%) [S1, S2]. A deposit puts something at stake, and appointments secured with one were missed 2.2% of the time [S3]. An easy way to cancel or move the booking turns a silent no-show into a slot you can still fill.
What a missed slot really costs

Take a salon with 120 appointments a week at an average of $60 each. These two figures are an example to show the method, not a benchmark. At the 10.5% no-show rate seen with no reminder and no deposit [S1], that salon loses about 12.6 appointments and $756 a week. At the 4.6% rate seen with a text and an email reminder [S2], it loses about 5.5 appointments and $331. Put your own weekly bookings and average price into the same sum before you decide which fix comes first.
The money is only part of it. The hour you set aside for a client who never comes cannot be sold again, and the client who wanted that slot was told you were full.

Reminders are the fix to start with, because they cost the client nothing and ask nothing of them. Send them for every service, not only the long ones, and send them from the booking system so nobody at the front desk has to remember. Chapter 3 shows when to send them and gives message templates that clients answer.

A deposit changes the decision: a client who has paid part of the price has a reason to show up or to tell you early. You may worry that asking for money up front will scare clients away, yet 69.9% of the 312 owners who take deposits told us it had not cost them bookings [S6]. Start with your longest and most expensive services, where an empty slot hurts most. Chapter 2 covers how much to ask for and how to word the policy.
Fix 3: Make cancelling easier than not showing up

Give clients a link in every reminder to cancel or move the booking themselves, at any hour. A cancellation two days ahead is a slot you can offer to someone else; a no-show is a slot you lose. Chapter 4 helps you write a cancellation policy clients respect, and chapter 5 shows how a waitlist refills the slots they free up.

Turn on automatic reminders for every service first. Then add a deposit to your longest appointments and watch your no-show rate for a month before you extend it. In Example Booking Software, both are settings on each service, and the next two chapters walk through them step by step.
